claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A transformer-based surrogate can fuse compositional descriptors, lower-fidelity simulation outputs, and microstructural image features.
The proposed model can accurately predict Young's modulus for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed model can accurately predict yield strength for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed model can accurately predict fracture toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed predictions apply under both tensile and fracture-testing conditions.
Grain-boundary chemistry, local phase distributions, and compositional fluctuations mediate the relationship between multiscale inputs and mechanical behavior.
Transformer self-attention can capture complex relationships among compositional and structural features across scales.
Learning key descriptors can replace or bypass computationally intensive first-principles calculations when predicting mechanical behavior.
The learned descriptors can efficiently predict deformation behavior and fracture initiation.
Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness will be predicted within 5–10% error.
The surrogate will provide a 10–100× computational speed improvement over high-fidelity ab initio and CALPHAD methods.
Physically based prediction of metallic yield strength can require complicated and lengthy calculations, making surrogate models attractive for large alloy sets.
Conventional machine-learning approaches insufficiently capture fracture toughness arising from a complex hierarchical structure.
The model may become unreliable when new samples contain microstructural or chemical variations outside the training domain.
Prediction performance depends on the quality and comprehensiveness of the multiscale training data.
The stated 5–10% error and 10–100× speedup estimates are based on analogous transformer implementations in related materials systems.
The hypothesis is prospectively testable using blinded, newly fabricated specimens followed by standardized tensile and fracture testing.
Prediction errors above 10% or a speedup below 10× are specified as decisive falsification thresholds.
Consistent failures on samples with features outside the training domain are specified as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes out-of-training-domain microstructures from the model's reliable scope, but the falsification rule treats failures on those same out-of-domain samples as evidence against the hypothesis. A valid falsification benchmark should primarily test specimens within the prespecified applicability domain.
